title: SLO-driven autoscale policy framework: metric harmonization and safety guards
creator: Liam Chen
description: Goal: Design and implement an autoscaling policy engine for Dedicated capacity that uses harmonized target metrics (SLO-driven), multiple scaling algorithms (reactive, predictive, PID/target tracking), and explicit safety limits to guarantee throughput and protect cost and reliability. This ticket covers the policy abstraction, metric definitions and weighting, the safety guard layer (min/max, cooldowns, circuit breakers), and integration points with the existing orchestration and telemetry layers. Deliverables: policy schema, algorithm selection logic, simulation harness, canary rollout plan, dashboarding and alerts, and runbook updates.
acceptance_criteria: Policy schema implemented and validated in staging
At least two scaling algorithms available behind a feature flag (reactive threshold and predictive forecasting)
Safety guards enforce min/max capacity, cooldown windows, and a cost budget cap in simulation
E2E simulation shows <1.5x overshoot on rapid ramp tests and meets p99 latency SLO for target workloads
Documentation and console UI hooks for choosing target metric and safety profile
work_log: 2025-02-28 - Ticket created by Liam Chen outlining scope and initial metric candidates (p99 latency, sustained throughput, GPU utilization, queue length)
2025-03-01 - Sync with SRE (R. Morales) and PM (S. Gupta); agreed to make SLO p99 latency primary metric for low-latency workloads and throughput per-GPU primary for batch workloads
2025-03-02 - Prototype metric harmonizer: compositeScore = w1*p99_norm + w2*util_norm + w3*queue_norm. Early tests show composite score reduces false positives compared to single-metric rule
2025-03-03 - Design review with runtime team: decided to support three algorithm families: threshold/step, PID-like target tracking, and ML predictive (ARIMA/prophet prototype) behind flags
2025-03-04 - Safety guard checklist drafted: min_replicas, max_replicas, cooldown_seconds, warm_pool_target, cost_budget_per_hour, scale_rate_limit, emergency_fallback_model
2025-03-05 - Ran synthetic spike simulation with 10k QPS ramp; observed 1.3x transient overshoot with predictive enabled vs 1.6x with naive step scaling. Preparing canary plan.
decisions: Primary SLO: use p99 tail latency for latency-sensitive routes and throughput-per-GPU for throughput-first routes
Composite metric allowed for mixed workloads; weights configurable at route level
Algorithm selection is per-route with a tenant-level default; predictive algorithm must be gated behind feature flag and historical window requirement
Safety guards are mandatory and evaluated before scaling actions are applied (pre-flight checks)
tradeoffs: Predictive algorithms reduce overshoot but require storage of historical traffic and introduce complexity in failure modes
Aggressive scaling (short cooldowns) improves SLO adherence at the cost of higher spend and potential oscillation
Composite metrics reduce noisy triggers but add tuning surface and can mask single-point regressions (we mitigate via per-metric alerts)
open_questions: What default weight set should apply for compositeScore (suggested: p99:0.6, util:0.3, queue:0.1)?
What is the acceptable max_replicas multiplier above baseline for on-demand bursts (2x, 4x)?
Should warm pools be soft (best-effort) or hard-reserved capacity for enterprise SKUs?
What telemetry retention window is required for predictive models to function reliably (7d, 30d)?
implementation_notes: Expose policy as a JSON/YAML schema consumed by the policy engine in the control plane
Integrate metric harmonizer in the telemetry pipeline to emit normalized signals for each route
Add a pre-flight safety evaluator that rejects scaling actions violating cost or regional constraints
Implement canary rollout: feature flag + 5% tenant sample with extended logging and a kill switch
tests_and_validation: Unit tests for compositeScore and per-metric normalization
Integration test: end-to-end scale up/down in staging with synthetic traffic patterns
Chaos test: simulate predictor failure and verify fallback to threshold algorithm
Cost shock test: verify cost_budget caps prevent runaway scaling in worst-case scenarios
